docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
A local app: a Python server that reads DCS and serves a web interface, all shipped as a single .exe.

hotas_kneeboard/          FastAPI server (127.0.0.1 only)
  engine.py + lua/        engine reading the bindings
  pages.py                grouping per input and per layer, released positions
  dcs.py                  detection of DCS, of Saved Games, of the language; translation of the commands
  templates.py            format and library of the templates
  kneeboard.py            writing of the PNG pages
  dcs_config.py           changes to the DCS controls: refused while DCS runs, backup and restore, devices disabled or forgotten
  hat_views.py            removal at once of the 8 generic hat views (preview, selection, reading again)
  generic_buttons.py      removal at once of the generic buttons of the devices without buttons (same pattern)
  lua_tables.py + lua/    reading and writing DCS's Lua files, with the game's serializer
  settings.py             settings (%APPDATA%/HOTAS Kneeboard/settings.json)
  i18n.py + locales/      the server's messages in French and in English
  app.py                  HTTP routes
  library/                the shipped templates
web/                      Vue 3 + TypeScript + Vite + PrimeVue + VueUse interface
  src/render/             building the pages as SVG (screen, PNG and PDF start from the same SVG)
  src/editor/             template editor
  src/locales/            the interface's texts in French and in English (src/lib/i18n.ts)
scripts/                  conversion of the templates, comparison with DCS, checking of the templates
packaging/                building the exe (PyInstaller)

The pages are built in the browser: the PNG goes through a canvas, the PDF through jsPDF. The server only writes the PNG files; there is neither Chromium nor Cairo to ship.

The DCS controls files (Saved Games/DCS/Config/Input) are only changed by dcs_config.py, and always through guarded_write. It refuses while DCS runs, since the game writes these files again when it saves its controls. Before writing, it zips the whole folder into %APPDATA%/HOTAS Kneeboard/backups/ (the last 20 zips are kept); a restore replaces the folder with a single rename, after backing up the current state.

A DCS file is read by running it with luae.exe, which gives back its value as JSON, and written again with the game's Scripts/Serializer.lua, in binary (DCS writes LF line endings). Read then written again this way, the 88 files of a real Config/Input (diffs, modifiers.lua, disabled.lua) are identical byte for byte. ED's serializer cannot be redistributed: the test fixture has its own, and test_lua_tables.py checks that it writes the same bytes as the real one when DCS_TEST_LUA is the bin/luae.exe of an install.

docs.title: The reading engine
docs.text:
A Saved Games/DCS/Config/Input/<profile>/joystick/<device>.diff.lua file only holds the user's changes against the module's defaults. The real bindings are the defaults (Lua programs of the module) plus this diff, merged by rules that live in DCS World/Scripts/Input/Data.lua.

lua/effective_bindings.lua reproduces this logic and runs with the Lua 5.1 interpreter shipped with DCS (bin/luae.exe): the defaults are run as they are, and the commands' "hashes" are computed exactly as in the game. It comes from VEAF/joystick-diagrams-dcs-world-plugin, where its rules are documented (the plugin's PRD, VEAF/joystick-diagrams-dcs-world-plugin#1). Additions specific to this repository:

  • the aircraft type of each profile, read in the make_flyable calls of the module's entry.lua: it is the name of the kneeboard folder (A-10C II → A-10C_2);
  • the name the DCS controls screen gives each profile (display_name), the string the name.lua of its folder returns ("AH-64D Pilot" for AH-64D_BLK_II_PLT); the server translates it like the commands, and tells two profiles with the same name apart by their folder;
  • a device without a base profile, or of a module not installed, shows what its diff adds rather than nothing;
  • the removal of bindings (remove records, key or axis by their last field): the engine then computes the diff of each device concerned again as DCS does when saving (saveDeviceProfile), against the module's defaults without the diff shipped with it; a removed axis is written as DCS writes it (["removed"] = { [1] = { ["key"] = "JOY_RZ" } }, compared with a diff saved by the game);
  • the combos whose key is not an input of the device are left out, as DCS does (getKeyBelongToDevice): the C-130J's joystick profile declares keyboard keys;
  • the devices asked for by device records are computed in the module profiles where they have no diff too (the module's defaults, marked extra), and scope installed adds every installed module profile: that is what allows creating a diff where there is none;
  • each binding the user's diff adds or changes is marked from_diff, unless the diff shipped by the module for this device places it too: DCS copies that diff into the user's at the first save, what it places is therefore still the module's; those are marked from_module_diff;
  • base_file says where the defaults come from: the module's profile for this device, or its default.lua, the profile of "any joystick" when it has none; with both marks, that is the origin in the Bindings window (app.binding_origin: user, device, generic);
  • each recomputation gives back the number of bindings actually removed (removed); remove_bindings does not write a device again where none was.

The 8 hat views (hat_views.py) come from Config/Input/Aircrafts/common_joystick_binding.lua, included in the defaults of every module: they are recognised by the (hash, key) pair, the same in every module (dnilp34u214… for JOY_BTN_POV1_U…), never by the name shown. A device is offered by default if no hat binding (a key holding POV) comes from a diff, in any module: a module's defaults on a hat (the turret of ground_unit, the Ka-50's Shkval) do not count. Only the views coming from the defaults are removed; a new diff is only created for a device that Logs/dcs.log names, under that name. After writing, the preview is computed again: a view expected that is still there, or a number removed other than expected, is reported. Checked on 2026-10-19 on a faithful copy of a real Saved Games: 505 views removed over 160 device × module pairs (44 files created among them), reading again without difference, and effective bindings identical before and after apart from these views.

The generic buttons (generic_buttons.py) are the key bindings of a device whose base is default.lua, neither from_diff nor from_module_diff, on the devices the user marked as without buttons (Settings.buttonless_devices, names without GUID): DCS writes nowhere how many buttons a device has. The default scope is the modules where the device has a diff; all_modules adds every installed module (a diff created where there is none). Preview, single backup, reading again and differences are those of the hat views. A binding whose hash still names an iCommand… symbol (@), for lack of a learnt number, cannot be removed: its removal cannot be written as DCS writes it; the preview shows it apart (unknown), the bindings API marks it removable: false. Checked on 2026-10-19 on a copy of a real Saved Games: rudder pedals, 20 bindings in 9 modules, reading again as previewed, no axis touched; the 5 of ground_unit (turret, secondary fire) stay apart.

The recomputation covers keys (combos added, removed) and axes (plus the combos whose filter changed, compared as DCS does: default values of createAxisFilter, detent values never compared); the force feedback diff is copied from the file, read by lua_tables. A diff entry that no longer matches any command disappears, as when DCS saves; an entry whose command has an unknown iCommand number makes the write refused, so as not to lose the binding. An empty diff is deleted, as DCS does: the device falls back on the module's defaults, and on the diff shipped with it if there is one. Proven on 2026-10-19 against DCS: 4 views removed by hand in the controls screen (Orion stick, F-16C_50), the same operation made by the app on the same starting state gives the same file byte for byte, and so do the rudder pedals DCS wrote again on the way. On a faithful copy of a real Saved Games (community commands included), writing the 57 diffs again without removing anything leaves the bindings of 55 devices identical; the other 2 only held stale entries, their file is deleted and they fall back on the defaults, with no effect in the game.

The values that go to the engine pass through its standard input, one record per line, fields separated by tabs: engine._loader_input refuses any value holding a tab or a line break, which would add records of its own (an install elsewhere, whose Lua files the interpreter would run). The routes that get a module name only accept a configured module, and the server refuses any /api/ request marked Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site, reads included: a page of another site must not be able to start the engine.

luae.exe opens files through the C library, limited to 260 characters on Windows: a diff with a longer path is not read. The recomputation would take it for a missing diff; dcs_config.new_diffs therefore refuses to write when the user's diff exists and the engine did not read it.

The command names shown are translated by l10n/<language>/LC_MESSAGES/input.mo, as the game does, English included ("Trim: Nose Up" shows as "Trim Hat - NOSE UP" in the A-10C II).

Any change to the engine or to pages.py is checked against the "MAKE HTML" export of the DCS controls screen:

uv run python scripts/compare_make_html.py "A-10C II" "F-16C_50"

The last line is the verdict; the export only covers the devices plugged in when it was made.

docs.title: The languages
docs.text:
The interface, the server's messages and the documentation exist in French and in English, the same way as in VEAF-Mission-Creation-Tools. The command names come from DCS's l10n files (the "Commands language" setting) and do not go through this.

  • The texts are in flat JSON catalogs, one per language: web/src/locales/<language>.json for the interface, hotas_kneeboard/locales/<language>.json for the server. A dotted key (settings.title), parameters in braces ({device}); a plural is a <key>.one / <key>.other pair (in French, zero is singular). English is the reference: a key missing from another catalog falls back on English, then on the key itself.
  • In the interface, t('key', { parameters }) and tn('key', count) (web/src/lib/i18n.ts); a text holding markup (a <code>, a link) goes through the Tr component, which puts each named slot where the translation puts {name}. lang is reactive: what reads it is drawn again when the language changes.
  • The interface language is a setting (ui_language: fr, en, or null for the browser's), applied at once; a copy in localStorage avoids showing the other language while the settings are read.
  • The server answers in the language of the request: the interface sends its own in Accept-Language, and i18n.LanguageMiddleware sets it for the time of the request (a ContextVar, seen from synchronous routes too). Out of a request (the console of the exe), it is HOTAS_KNEEBOARD_LANG, else Windows' display language, else English. t("key", name=value) in hotas_kneeboard/i18n.py.
  • The kneeboard pages speak the commands' language, not the interface's (pageLanguage): in French when DCS is in French, in English otherwise, so that a page does not mix two languages. The same holds for the SRS and VectorXR actions drawn on them: the interface asks for /api/programs in that language.
  • The tests check that both catalogs have the same keys and the same parameters, and that every key the code asks for exists (web/src/lib/__tests__/i18n.test.ts, tests/test_i18n.py). The Python tests read the messages in French (tests/conftest.py), test_i18n.py checks the English ones.

A new text goes into both catalogs, in the same move as the code; a text written straight into a component or an error message is an oversight.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
Python (with uv):

uv sync
uv run ruff check . && uv run ruff format --check .
DCS_TEST_LUA="C:/jeux/DCS World/bin/luae.exe" uv run pytest

Without DCS_TEST_LUA, the engine tests look for a Lua 5.1 in the PATH and are skipped if there is none; the CI uses lua5.1.

Interface (with npm):

cd web
npm ci
npx vue-tsc -b && npx vitest run
npm run build

npm run build writes the interface into hotas_kneeboard/web/, ignored by git.

Running for development:

uv run hotas-kneeboard --no-browser

then npm run dev in web/ for the interface reloaded on the fly (the /api calls are relayed to the server on port 8642). HOTAS_KNEEBOARD_DATA changes the folder of the user's settings and templates, so as not to touch your own while trying things.

Building the exe:

pwsh packaging/build.ps1

It produces dist/HOTAS-Kneeboard.exe.

docs.title: The documentation site
docs.text:
The documentation is published on https://veaf.github.io/hotas-kneeboard/ (the repository's GitHub Pages, gh-pages branch) with MkDocs Material and mike, like VEAF-Mission-Creation-Tools'. The pages are those of docs/, except docs/agents/, which is meant for the Claude sessions.

It is in French and in English, with the mkdocs-static-i18n plugin, as VMCT does:

  • page.md is the French page (the default language, at the root of the site), page.en.md the English page (under en/); a new page is written in both languages and goes into the nav of mkdocs.yml, written in English, with its translation in nav_translations.
  • A picture name.en.png takes the place of name.png on the English site; without it, the English site shows the French picture.
  • README.md holds the English then the French, from <a id="fr"></a>; at build time, scripts/mkdocs_hooks.py makes the two home pages of it, docs/index.en.md and docs/index.md (ignored by git).
  • The links of an English page aim at the English pages (guide-utilisateur.en.md): that way they work on GitHub as on the site.

Publishing:

  • A push to develop publishes the "dev" version; as long as no release is out, the site's address opens that one.
  • A release (a push to main) publishes the version of pyproject.toml and marks it "latest", which the site's address opens from then on. It is the push to main that triggers it, not the vX.Y.Z tag: release.yml creates the tag with GitHub Actions' token, and an event made with that token starts no other workflow.
  • Each PR builds the site with --strict: a link to a missing page or an anchor that does not exist makes the CI fail. The anchors are GitHub's, accents included (#vérifier-la-numérotation-sur-le-périphérique): a link works on both. Each language has its own, taken from its headings (#check-the-numbering-on-the-device in English); --strict catches a link a reworded heading broke. A link to a file outside the site (CHANGELOG.md, docs/agents/) is written as a full GitHub address.

Seeing the site locally, reloaded on each change:

uv run --group docs mkdocs serve

docs.title: The screenshots
docs.text:
The pictures of docs/images/ are taken in the app itself by scripts/doc_screenshots.py, which drives the installed Edge with Playwright. The script only looks: it opens the screens and the windows, runs the previews ("Search"), and clicks on nothing that writes to DCS. It sets the interface and commands language, and ticks the rudder pedals in "Devices without buttons", which writes the app's settings: it is therefore run on an app started with a throwaway HOTAS_KNEEBOARD_DATA, in a first terminal:

$env:HOTAS_KNEEBOARD_DATA = "$env:TEMP\hk-shots"; uv run hotas-kneeboard --port 8654 --no-browser

then, in a second terminal, the French screenshots, then the English ones:

$env:HOTAS_KNEEBOARD_DATA = "$env:TEMP\hk-shots"; uv run --with playwright python scripts/doc_screenshots.py
$env:HOTAS_KNEEBOARD_DATA = "$env:TEMP\hk-shots"; uv run --with playwright python scripts/doc_screenshots.py --lang en
  • --lang en writes name.en.png beside each name.png, the interface and the commands in English; the script finds the buttons by their text in the interface's catalog, which a reworded label therefore does not break.
  • The pictures show the devices of the PC that takes them: the script picks the A-10C II, the WinWing Orion stick and the T-Pendular rudder pedals; elsewhere, change MODULE, STICK and RUDDER at the top of the script.
  • The Windows user's name and the throwaway folder are replaced on screen with those of an ordinary pilot (C:\Users\Pilote, %APPDATA%\HOTAS Kneeboard).
  • Screen names as arguments (ecran, editeur…) retake only those.
  • The screenshots are retaken when the interface changes, at the latest in the release PR: look at each picture again before committing it.

docs.title: Lots, tickets, branches and releases
docs.text:
The tracking follows the organisation of VEAF-Mission-Creation-Tools, with GitHub issues in place of the .backlog/ files; the details are in docs/agents/issue-tracker.md.

  • The product's PRD is #1; its lots are its sub-issues.
  • A lot is an issue labelled lot, titled <LOT-ID> — …, its PRD in the body; its tickets are its sub-issues, labelled ticket, cut with /to-tickets before the code.
  • The status is a label: ⬜ ready · 🔄 in-progress · 🧑 waiting-human · ⏸ paused; closed = ✅ done or 🚫 won't fix (details).
  • develop is the default branch and gets the work, main only gets releases.
  • A lot is a feature/, fix/ or chore/<LOT-ID> branch made from develop, and a single PR to develop, which closes its tickets and the lot. Each lot adds its entries at the end of [Unreleased] in CHANGELOG.md, without touching the version.
  • A release is a PR from develop to main that raises the version in pyproject.toml and hotas_kneeboard/__init__.py (the two must be equal) and moves [Unreleased] under that number. On merge, the CI builds the exe on Windows and publishes the vX.Y.Z release; a merge without a version change publishes nothing. If the interface changed since the previous release, the PR also retakes the screenshots. Its notes are RELEASE_NOTES.md, rewritten at each release as for VMCT: in French, for the pilots (what changes for them, not the plumbing), the title ending with the version number; the CI refuses to publish if the title does not carry the version, and adds under the title the link to the documentation of that version.
  • The CI (Python and interface tests) runs on each PR and on each push to develop and main.

docs.title: Repository rules
docs.text:
• The interface, the server's messages and the documentation are in French and in English (see The languages); the code and its comments in English.
  • The command names shown are the game's, translated; never show the raw names of the Lua files.
  • The templates keep their credit and their license.
  • The server only accepts the 127.0.0.1 and localhost hosts, and refuses writes coming from another site.

docs.title: Template editor
docs.text: A template is the drawing of a device and the position of each button on it. The editor is there to draw a device that has none, to correct an existing template, and to check it on the real hardware.

docs.title: Opening the editor
docs.text:
• From a device's page: Create (it has no template) or Edit (it has one). The template saved will then be this device's.
  • Or with the pencil, at the top of the screen, for a template without a given device.

Pages brings back the main screen; the editor warns you if changes are not saved.

docs.title: Starting from a picture
docs.text:
Drag a photo or a drawing of the device onto the window (PNG, JPG or SVG), or click Picture…. A picture seen from the front, on a light background, with room around it for the labels, gives the best pages.

You can also start from an existing template (Start from a template…):

  • if it is this device's template, you correct it, and your version comes before the library's (the "replaces the library's" badge recalls it);
  • if it is another device's template, the editor makes a new template of it for yours, without touching the other one;
  • a template that names no device (most converted templates, chosen by hand) is corrected in place, and learns your device's name.

docs.title: Placing the inputs
docs.text:
An input is a button, a direction of a hat or an axis, as DCS names it. It has a box (where the command is written) and, if you want, a marker (a dot on the button, linked to the box by a line).

  • Drag ＋ Input onto the picture, or press N then click on the button: a marker is laid, its box beside it.
  • Drag the marker or the box; resize the box by its orange corner.
  • Choose the input in the list (Buttons 1 to 128, Hats 1 to 4 in the eight directions, Axes). Choosing an input already placed swaps the two.
  • With / No marker, 2nd box (the same input drawn in two places, on two views of the device), Duplicate (on the next button), Delete.

docs.title: Identifying a button by pressing it
docs.text: Identify (I key), then press the device's button: the editor recognises the input and gives it to the selected input (or to the next one you place). It goes through the browser's Gamepad API, which numbers the buttons its own way: check the number it gives, the list stays the reference. If the device has just appeared (the browser only shows a controller after a first press), the editor asks you to press a second time. Hats are not recognised: choose them in the list.

docs.title: Check the numbering on the device
docs.text:
Check (V key), then press every button of the device, one after the other:

  • if the button has its box, the box lights up;
  • otherwise, the editor asks you to click on the picture where the button is.

The buttons seen show as you go, in green when they have their box. Once every button is tried and the boxes corrected, enter your nickname and click Mark as checked: the page will no longer say "numbering not checked".

docs.title: Cutting into two pages
docs.text: For a drawing too wide for one page (a throttle and its base), Cut into two pages adds a blue line. Drag it through a white area, between two parts of the drawing: it must cut neither the device nor a box. Do not cut removes it.

docs.title: Preview, saving, sharing
docs.text:
• Preview (P key) shows the template with the real bindings of a module: choose the module and the device in the list.
  • Save (Ctrl+S) puts the template in your library, %APPDATA%\HOTAS Kneeboard\templates\. The device you opened it for uses it at once.
  • Save as new makes one more template of it, whatever the template it started from.
  • Export downloads the template as a file (.zip); Import… (or dragging and dropping the file) adds it to the library of another PC.
  • Delete the template removes one of your templates; if it was your version of a library template, the library's comes back.

To give a checked template to everyone, see Templates.

docs.title: Editor shortcuts
docs.text: Key Action N Place an input (then click on the picture) I Identify by pressing the button V Check: press every button of the device Del Delete the selection Ctrl + D Duplicate on the next button ← ↑ → ↓ Move (Shift: by 10) Ctrl + Z / Ctrl + Y Undo / redo + − 0 Zoom, fit P Preview with real bindings Ctrl + S Save Esc Stop placing, deselect

docs.title: The format
docs.text:
A template is a folder that holds template.json and the device's picture (SVG, PNG or JPG), without any label on it.

{
  "format": 1,
  "name": "Thrustmaster Warthog - Throttle",
  "devices": ["Throttle - HOTAS Warthog"],
  "image": "background.svg",
  "size": [828, 1169],
  "inputs": {
    "JOY_BTN16": { "box": [330, 28, 90, 30] },
    "JOY_BTN1": { "box": [205, 666, 180, 30], "anchor": [545, 706] },
    "JOY_BTN5": { "box": [10, 10, 80, 20], "more_boxes": [[400, 10, 80, 20]] }
  },
  "credits": { "author": "Joystick Diagrams contributors", "source": "https://github.com/…", "license": "GPL-2.0" },
  "checked": { "by": "David", "date": "2026-10-19" },
  "split_at": [566]
}
Field Meaning devices The DCS names of the devices that use this template, without the GUID in braces; the match ignores case. Empty: the template is chosen by hand. size The picture's frame: width and height, from 1 to 20,000. inputs One input per DCS name: JOY_BTN14, JOY_BTN_POV1_U (hat 1 up), JOY_X, JOY_RZ, JOY_SLIDER1… box The label's box: x, y, width, height, in the picture's frame. anchor Optional: the button's point, linked to the box by a line. more_boxes Optional: other boxes for the same input, when the device is drawn from several angles. checked Who checked the numbering on the real device, and when; null otherwise. split_at Optional: the x positions where the drawing is cut into several kneeboard pages.

A released position (JOY_BTN17_OFF) has no box of its own: it is written in the one of JOY_BTN17.

docs.title: The library
docs.text:
The app looks for templates in two places:

  1. those shipped with it (hotas_kneeboard/library/ in the repository);
  2. yours, in %APPDATA%\HOTAS Kneeboard\templates\, made with the editor or imported.

A template of yours comes before a shipped template with the same id (the folder's name), and before it for the automatic match of a device.

docs.title: The Joystick Diagrams templates
docs.text:
The 45 shipped templates are converted from those of Joystick Diagrams (Robert Cox, alias Rexeh, and its contributors, GPL v2). They are draw.io drawings exported as SVG, with a box per input holding a token (Button_14, POV_1_U, AXIS_X) that Joystick Diagrams replaces with the command.

scripts/convert_jd_templates.py converts them:

  • it removes the token boxes from the picture and keeps the rest: the photo, the leader lines, the notes, the credit;
  • it replaces draw.io's HTML text with plain SVG text, which the browser can draw into a PNG and a PDF;
  • it records the position of each box under the input's DCS name, recognising the different spellings of the tokens;
  • it takes from scripts/jd_templates.json the template's id, the known DCS names, the numbering corrections (the Warthog throttle's coolie goes from hat 2 to hat 1), the cut lines and the checking state.
uv run python scripts/convert_jd_templates.py <path of joystick-diagrams>/templates

It shows, for each template, the number of inputs found and the tokens it did not recognise.

Good to know:

  • the DCS names are only known for 20 templates; the others are chosen by hand, once, and the app remembers it;
  • the WinWing names come from the list of devices DCS recognises (Scripts\Input\DefaultAssignments.lua) and from the profiles shipped by the modules, old firmware names included (WINWING THROTTLE BASE2 + …); recent firmwares are named WINCTRL …, and only those seen on a real PC are known;
  • a name shared by two templates is put on neither: the left- or right-handed T.16000M, the JGRIP-F16 with or without the vibration kit, the F/A-18 throttle with or without axes, the F/A-18 UFC and HUD plugged together (WINWING UFC1 + HUD1);
  • the Virpil templates have no DCS name, and will have none: the name Windows gives a Virpil device is the base's ("VPC Stick MT-50CM3"), not the grip's on it, and Virpil's configuration software lets you change it; choose your grip's template by hand;
  • the numbering of the converted templates is the one Joystick Diagrams drew, not necessarily the device's: the Orion JGRIP-F16's has no box for the trigger (button 1) nor for buttons 2 and 21 to 29;
  • no template is marked checked yet.

docs.title: Checking a template
docs.text:
With the device plugged in:

  1. uv run python scripts/check_templates.py lists, for your devices, the inputs bound in DCS that have no box on their template (the generic views DCS puts on the hat of every device are ignored). Without the device, --device "Throttle - HOTAS Warthog" (the DCS name, without GUID, repeatable option) makes the same check on the bindings DCS gives it by default in each installed module (your changes count where you made some), without what a module gives any joystick for lack of a profile for that one (the axes and the hat of its default.lua): it finds the missing boxes, not the numbering errors, which only the real device shows.
  2. In the app, open the device's page, Edit, then Check: press every button, move or add the boxes (see the editor).
  3. Enter your nickname, Mark as checked, save: your version comes before the library's, on your PC.

docs.title: Adding a template to the library
docs.text:
For everyone to have the checked template, or a device Joystick Diagrams did not draw:

  1. in the editor, Export the template;
  2. unzip the file into hotas_kneeboard/library/<id>/ (the same id as the shipped template it corrects, or a new one);
  3. for a converted template, put "maintained": true on its entry of scripts/jd_templates.json: the conversion will then leave it as it is;
  4. offer it as a PR on the repository (see Development).

docs.title: First start
docs.text:
Run HOTAS-Kneeboard.exe. A console opens with the address of the app (http://127.0.0.1:8642/) and your browser opens on it. The app runs as long as the console is open: closing it quits the app. Running the exe again while it is already running simply opens the browser on the running one.

The app finds by itself:

  • the DCS install, in the Windows registry (HKCU\Software\Eagle Dynamics\DCS World);
  • the Saved Games\DCS (or DCS.openbeta) folder of your profile;
  • the game's language, to show the commands as DCS shows them.

The DCS badge at the top is green when everything is found; hover over it to see the folders. If something is missing, a banner says so, with a direct way to the settings.

The app reads your files without changing them, except when you ask it to change your DCS controls (see DCS controls): it then backs everything up before writing. Otherwise, it only writes the kneeboard pages, and its own settings in %APPDATA%\HOTAS Kneeboard\.

The interface is in English or in French: by default it follows your browser's language, and the settings let you choose (see Settings).

docs.title: The screen
docs.text:
Three columns, from left to right.

Modules. Every controls profile you set up in DCS (an aircraft, a helicopter, the interface layer…), under the name the game's controls screen gives it ("AH-64D Pilot", "F/A-18C"), in alphabetical order. Under the name, the profile's folder in Saved Games\DCS\Config\Input when it differs (AH-64D_BLK_II_PLT), and the aircraft's kneeboard folder; on the right, the number of devices exported out of the number of devices shown. Two profiles with the same name (DCS sometimes keeps the old folder of a renamed module, like Mi-24P Pilot and Mi-24P_pilot) are told apart by their folder, in brackets. The filter searches the name, the folder and the aircraft type. A module DCS does not find in your install is marked "module not installed": only your changes are known, not its defaults.

Devices. The devices set up for this module. The checkbox includes the device in the exports or not; drag and drop changes the order of the pages. "template": the device has a drawing; "list": it has none, its page is a list of commands. The eye, when hovering over a row, hides the device in every module (see Settings).

The page. The page as it will be in the kneeboard, fitted to the room available. Above it: the template used (found automatically, or chosen by hand in the list, and then remembered), the button to Create it or Edit it in the editor, the display of the layers. A choice by hand holds for this device in every module; the first entry of the list, Automatic, names the template recognised by the device's name and goes back to it. When the template chosen by hand is not that one (the stick drawn with the picture of the throttle), the chosen by hand badge says so: its tooltip names the template recognised, a click goes back to it. At the bottom right, the zoom: whole page, full width, more or less (or Ctrl+wheel).

The line between two columns can be dragged to widen or narrow the modules column or the devices one; the app remembers it, and a double click on the line puts back the default width.

In the top bar, the book opens this documentation, the one of your version of the app and in the interface's language, in a new tab; the shortcuts window (?) leads there too.

docs.title: Reading a page
docs.text:
• A label per bound button, laid on the box of the drawing. The text shrinks to fit; if it really does not fit, the box gets longer.
  • The dotted boxes are inputs of the drawing without a command: free buttons.
  • A two-position switch fits on one label: "LG Handle - UP / DN". A released position alone (without a pressed position) is written in italics, after "released:".
  • Modifier layers. A command bound with a modifier (the Warthog's "Paddle", for example) shows in the same label, in colour, after a small badge ("P"). The legend is at the bottom of the page ("P = Paddle"). With "Per layer", each layer has its own page.
  • Off template. A command bound to an input that has no box on the drawing is listed under the drawing: nothing gets lost. It is often the sign of a template to check (see the editor).
  • "numbering not checked": the template comes from the library and nobody has checked yet, on the real device, that every button lands in the right box.
  • Drawings too wide for one page (the WinWing Orion throttles, base and handles) are cut into two pages, where the template says; on screen, the two halves are side by side if the window is wide enough.
  • A device without a template has a list page: the input ("Button 14", "Hat 1 ↑", "Axis X"), then the command. If the list is long, it goes on onto a following page.

The words the app writes itself on the pages ("released:", the template's credit line, the head of a list page) are in French when the commands are in French, in English otherwise: a page never mixes two languages.

docs.title: The buttons of other programs
docs.text:
A button may serve something other than DCS: SRS's push to talk, VectorXR's overlay, a VoiceAttack voice command. These buttons show on the pages, beside the DCS commands, each program in its colour and with its badge ("SRS", "VXR" for VectorXR); the legend is at the bottom of the page. They are on every page, even with "Per layer": these programs ignore DCS's modifiers.

  • SRS is read directly, never touching its settings. Each aircraft has its SRS profile: the module's is found by its name ("F-16" for "F-16C_50", "A-10C" for "A-10C II"), otherwise it is the default profile. The Other programs button, at the top of the page, lets you choose another one for this module, or none; the choice is remembered.
  • VectorXR is read directly too, and its buttons hold for every module. Only what is used in DCS counts: a disabled profile, or a profile of another game, does not show. A VectorXR module saved turned off (PivotXR, DepthXR…) keeps its buttons: it turns on again in flight, and its DCS profiles are used all the same. The label names the profile when there are several ("PivotXR snapviews: view Right MFD").
  • Another program is entered by hand, from Other programs: the program's name, the button (in the list, or by pressing it with Identify) and what it does. The entries are edited and deleted in the same place.

In the settings, the Other programs tab gives SRS's folder (found in the Windows registry, to enter if it is not), what was read, and lets you hide a program from the pages or change its colour.

docs.title: To the kneeboard
docs.text:
Kneeboard (or Ctrl+E) writes the module's pages into Saved Games\DCS\Kneeboard\<aircraft>\, one per ticked device (two for a cut drawing, one per layer if you chose "Per layer").

  • The folder's name is DCS's aircraft type (A-10C_2 for the "A-10C II" profile), read in the module: it is the one the game looks at.
  • The pages are named HOTAS - <module> - 01 <device>.png, in the order of the list.
  • A new export replaces the pages of the same module, and only those: your own pages stay, and so do the pages of another seat of the same aircraft (the pilot and AI menu profiles of the AH-64D share the AH-64D_BLK_II folder).
  • The export is all or nothing: if a page cannot be written (a picture open in another program, for example), the previous pages stay in place.
  • A profile that is not an aircraft (the interface layer) has no kneeboard.

The pages show in this aircraft's kneeboard at the next mission. Their height is set in the settings (1024 pixels by default); the width follows the drawing's proportions.

Every module at once: the arrow beside Kneeboard, then Every module (or Shift+E). Each aircraft of the list that has at least one device ticked gets its pages, as if you exported it by hand; the profiles that are not aircraft (Default, UiLayer) are skipped. A window shows how far the export has got ("Module 7 of 20", the module's name, a bar); count about ten seconds for twenty modules. Stop stops at the end of the module in progress: the modules already written stay so, and the final message says how many were not. If a module fails, the others go on, and the final message says which one and why.

docs.title: As a PDF
docs.text: PDF (or Ctrl+P) downloads a PDF of the same pages, one A4 page per page, at about 200 dots per inch. The arrow beside it, Every module (or Shift+P), makes a single PDF, HOTAS - every module.pdf, module after module in the order of the list, with the same aircraft as for the kneeboard; each page carries the name of its module at its head. The same window shows the progress; Stop then writes no PDF at all, a PDF of part of the modules would pass for the whole.

docs.title: DCS controls
docs.text:
The slider button, at the top, opens the DCS controls window: what the app can change in your controls, and the backups it makes before.

  • DCS must be closed. The game writes its controls files again when you save in its controls screen: the app refuses any change while DCS (or a dedicated server) is running.
  • Before each change, the whole Saved Games\DCS\Config\Input folder is backed up in a zip, in %APPDATA%\HOTAS Kneeboard\backups\. The last 20 backups are kept; Back up now makes one by hand.
  • Restore… puts your controls back exactly in the state of this backup, for every module: the files that appeared since are removed. The state before the restore is itself backed up first, at the top of the list: a restore is undone by restoring that one.

docs.title: Disabling a device
docs.text:
The Devices disabled in DCS list holds every known device: those set up in a module, and those DCS saw at its last two starts ("seen by DCS lately", read in Saved Games\DCS\Logs\dcs.log and dcs.log.old).

  • The switch disables the device like the "Disable" button of the game's controls screen: DCS ignores it in every module, and its controls are kept for when it is enabled again.
  • It is useful for a plugged device DCS does not need: a Bluetooth gamepad, a vJoy.
  • In a module's list of devices, a disabled device has the disabled badge.

docs.title: Forgetting an absent device
docs.text:
The Absent devices list shows the devices that have saved controls, but that DCS did not see at its last two starts: an uninstalled vJoy, a device renamed by an update of its driver, a stick sold on. It cannot tell them from a device simply unplugged those days: the choice is yours.

  • Forget… then Forget deletes the device's controls in every module, after a backup: a restore brings them back.
  • A device DCS saw lately is never offered, nor is a disabled device: plugged in, it might not show in DCS's log.
  • Without a DCS log, or if the log names no device, the list is empty: start DCS once, with the devices plugged in.

docs.title: Repairing the modifiers of a renamed device
docs.text:
A modifier ("Paddle", a lever of the stick held to change layer) is saved with the full name of its device. When a driver update renames the device (WinWing: "WINWING Orion Joystick Base 2" became "WINCTRL Orion Joystick Base Metal 2"), DCS no longer recognises it and ignores it without a word. The bindings that use it are still shown, in the game as here, but no longer work in flight.

  • The Modifiers section lists them, module by module, with the old and the new name; in the list of devices and on the page, the inactive modifier badge says so too.
  • A device is recognised by its GUID, the same before and after the renaming, and by the name DCS gave it at its last two starts (Saved Games\DCS\Logs\dcs.log): plug it in and start DCS once before repairing. A device simply unplugged is not reported.
  • Repair gives these modifiers the name DCS uses now, in every module, after a backup.
  • When DCS has ignored a modifier, it writes the modifiers file again without it at the next save, and deletes it if only the default settings are left. If a backup of the app still has this file, the module is offered with Bring back: the file comes back with the names repaired, only this file is written. If you deleted this file yourself, leave it.

docs.title: Removing the hat views
docs.text:
Every module puts the 8 slow views ("View Up slow", "View Down Left slow"…) on the first hat of every device: the rudder pedals, the ICP, the MFDs have them too, even if the game's controls screen does not always show them. With TrackIR or VR they are useless and clutter the pages; the Hat views section removes them at once.

  • Search computes the preview (a few seconds): each device concerned, the number of views, the modules (unfoldable) and the files that will be created.
  • By default, only the devices on whose hat you put nothing yourself, in any module, are ticked: the rudder pedals, the ICP, the MFDs, a throttle whose hat is not used. The others are listed greyed out, with what you put on their hat.
  • Every device, hats in use included makes them tickable too: only the 8 default views go, your own bindings on the hat stay.
  • Every installed module extends the removal to the modules you never set up: a controls file is created for each module and each device concerned. Without the option, only the modules that have a folder in Saved Games\DCS\Config\Input are touched.
  • A file is only created for a device DCS saw at its last two starts, under the exact name the game gives it; an absent device keeps its existing files, processed as well.
  • Remove… then Remove: a single backup for the whole operation, then the controls are read again and compared with the preview. "As previewed" means every view announced is gone; otherwise, each difference is listed.
  • The files are written again the way DCS saves them: an entry that no longer does anything (a default setting changed since an update of the module) disappears, as when you save in the game. A file that keeps no difference with the default settings is deleted, as DCS does: the device then no longer shows in this module of the app, nothing is lost.
  • To go back, restore the backup "before removing the hat views" in the list of backups.

docs.title: Devices without buttons
docs.text:
When a module has nothing for a device, DCS gives it the bindings of "any joystick": rudder pedals get a weapon release on button 2, nosewheel steering on 4, a view recenter on 5… buttons they do not have. DCS writes nowhere how many buttons a device has: you are the one who says it.

  1. Tick, in the list, the devices that have neither button nor hat (the rudder pedals); the app remembers it.
  2. Search: the preview gives, per device and per module, the generic buttons that would go.
  3. Remove… then Remove: a single backup before, the controls read again after writing and compared with the preview; Undo this removal restores the backup.

Only the button and hat bindings that come from this generic profile go: what you put on the device yourself, what the module has for this very hardware, and every axis stay. A binding whose DCS command number the app does not know (Combined Arms' secondary fire and turret) cannot be removed from here: the preview shows it apart, remove it in the game's controls screen. By default, only the modules where the device is set up are touched; the "Every installed module" option creates a file in each one, so that a new aircraft is already clean.

docs.title: Removing bindings
docs.text:
The Bindings button, above the page, lists every binding of the device in this module: the input ("Button 1", "Axis Z"), the modifier if there is one, the command, and its origin.

  • "your setup": you set it in the DCS controls screen;
  • "default for this device": the module has it for this very device (the Warthog in the A-10C, for example), including in the file it ships and that DCS copies into yours;
  • "generic default": the module has nothing for this device, and DCS gives it what it gives any joystick.

The generic defaults are often worth removing: that is where you see a button doing two things without knowing it, an "Engine Stop Right" of yours and the "Gun Trigger" the A-10C puts on button 1 of any joystick, or the throttle on a stick's Z axis.

  1. Tick the bindings to remove (buttons, hats or axes); the filter searches the input and the command.
  2. Delete (n), then Remove to confirm.
  3. The pages are read again without them. Undo, in the same window, restores the backup made just before.

As for the rest of this window, DCS must be closed, and the whole Config\Input is backed up first; the device's file is written again as DCS saves it, a default binding removed being written there as removed. The removal only holds for this module: the same command stays in the others.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
The cog wheel, at the top, opens the settings. They are saved in %APPDATA%\HOTAS Kneeboard\settings.json; the exact path is recalled at the bottom of the window.

General.

  • The interface language: the browser's by default (French if your browser is in French, English otherwise), or French or English as you choose. It applies at once, to the menus as to the app's messages, and to the documentation the book opens.
  • The DCS folders: left empty, they are found automatically.
  • The commands language: the game's by default, or another language shipped with DCS. The words the app writes itself on the pages ("released:", the template's credit line, the head of a list page) follow this language: in French when the commands are in French, in English otherwise, so that a page does not mix two languages.
  • The height of the kneeboard pages.
  • Cutting into two pages the drawings that have a cut line.

Devices. Every device seen in your modules, with the number of modules it is set up in. Untick a device to hide it everywhere: a vJoy, a device unplugged for good, a ghost duplicate. A hidden device leaves the lists, the counts and the exports, in every module; it applies at once. "N hidden: Show", at the bottom of the list of devices, shows them again (greyed out); the eye or the H key hides or shows them one by one.

Other programs. SRS's folder, the programs shown on the pages and their colour: see the buttons of other programs.

The rest is remembered as you go: devices exported, order of the pages, template chosen by hand, display of the layers, zoom, light or dark theme.

docs.title: Common problems
docs.text:
"DCS install not found" or "DCS Saved Games folder not found". Enter the folder in the settings: the one that holds bin\luae.exe for the install, the one that holds Config\Input for Saved Games.

A page does not match what you set in DCS. You changed your controls in DCS while the app was running: F5 reads the files again.

"module not installed" or "no base profile". DCS did not find the defaults of this module or of this device: the page only shows what your changes add.

A button lands in the wrong box, or a command is "off template". The template's numbering does not match your device: check it in the editor.

A device shows twice, or has a strange name ("… BOOT"). Windows saw it once under another name, and DCS kept its setup; hide it in the settings.

A binding with a modifier ("Paddle + …") does not work in flight. The device's driver may have renamed it: the page then has the "inactive modifier" badge. See Repairing the modifiers of a renamed device.

The pages do not show in the kneeboard. Restart the mission: DCS reads the kneeboard folder when loading. Check the folder given in the message after the export, and that you are flying the aircraft of this module.
